title: On complemented subspaces of \(L_1[0,1]\)
author: Antonio Acuaviva
abstract: We construct continuum many complemented subspaces of \(L_1[0,1]\), with no isomorphic embeddings between distinct members. Each has the Schur property but fails the Radon–Nikodým property, and none is isomorphic to a Banach lattice. We also construct a complemented subspace containing a copy of \(\ell_2\) but no copy of \(L_1[0,1]\). These results give a negative answer to the complemented-subspace question of Lindenstrauss and Rosenthal. The same construction yields \(2^{2^{\aleph_0}}\) proper norm-closed two-sided ideals in \(\mathcal L(L_1[0,1])\), each containing an infinite-rank projection.

1.

Introduction

−

Understanding the complemented subspaces of classical Banach spaces, and classifying them up to isomorphism, is one of the central problems in the geometry of Banach spaces. For the classical sequence spaces, the corresponding classification has a particularly simple answer. Pełczyński  proved that every infinite-dimensional complemented subspace of \(c_0\) is isomorphic to \(c_0\), and that every infinite-dimensional complemented subspace of \(\ell_p\), \(1\le p<\infty\), is isomorphic to \(\ell_p\). His decomposition method became a basic tool in the study of complemented subspaces. Lindenstrauss  subsequently established the corresponding result for \(\ell_\infty\).

For \(1<p<\infty\), \(p\ne2\), the familiar complemented subspaces of \(L_p[0,1]\) already include the five mutually nonisomorphic spaces  \[\ell_p,\qquad \ell_2,\qquad \ell_p\oplus\ell_2,\qquad \left(\bigoplus_{n=1}^{\infty}\ell_2\right)_{\ell_p},\qquad L_p[0,1].\] Rosenthal  showed that these examples do not exhaust the possibilities. For \(2<p<\infty\), he constructed new complemented spaces \(X_p\) generated by suitable independent mean-zero random variables. Schechtman  then obtained infinitely many isomorphism types. Bourgain, Rosenthal and Schechtman  developed these constructions further, using an ordinal index to obtain uncountably many pairwise nonisomorphic complemented subspaces of \(L_p[0,1]\) for every \(1<p<\infty\), \(p\ne2\). Their work shows how far the reflexive Lebesgue spaces are from the classification of the sequence spaces, although a full classification of their complemented subspaces remains unavailable.

The spaces \(L_1[0,1]\) and \(C[0,1]\) remain the most prominent examples of classical Banach spaces whose complemented subspaces are not yet fully understood. For \(L_1[0,1]\), the question of Lindenstrauss and Rosenthal  asks whether every infinite-dimensional complemented subspace is isomorphic to either \(\ell_1\) or \(L_1[0,1]\). This is the separable case of Pełczyński’s question  about complemented subspaces of \(L_1\)-spaces. Popov  surveys the problem and its partial solutions.

The metric version has a complete answer. Over the real field, Grothendieck’s theorem  shows that the range of a contractive projection on an \(L_1\)-space is linearly isometric to an \(L_1\)-space. Douglas  proved the converse for subspaces of \(L_1[0,1]\): every subspace linearly isometric to an \(L_1\)-space is the range of a contractive projection. The characterization holds over both scalar fields; see also . If the projection is also positive, its range is a closed sublattice .

Positivity alone, without a norm-one assumption, is enough for the isomorphic classification. The range of a positive projection on a Banach lattice admits an equivalent Banach lattice norm . A complemented subspace of an \(L_1\)-space that is isomorphic to a Banach lattice is necessarily isomorphic to an \(L_1\)-space . Consequently, every infinite-dimensional range of a positive projection on \(L_1[0,1]\) is isomorphic to \(\ell_1\) or \(L_1[0,1]\).

Pełczyński’s work  implies that every infinite-dimensional complemented subspace of \(L_1[0,1]\) contains a copy of \(\ell_1\) complemented in \(L_1[0,1]\). Lindenstrauss and Pełczyński  proved that such a subspace is isomorphic to \(\ell_1\) if it has an unconditional basis, and Lewis and Stegall  reached the same conclusion under the Radon–Nikodým property. In the other direction, Enflo and Starbird  proved that a complemented subspace containing a copy of \(L_1[0,1]\) must itself be isomorphic to \(L_1[0,1]\). Thus a counterexample must lie outside both of these established parts of the classification.

Popov  separates the problem into two questions: whether every infinite-dimensional complemented Schur subspace of \(L_1[0,1]\) is isomorphic to \(\ell_1\), and whether every complemented subspace without the Schur property is isomorphic to \(L_1[0,1]\). The constructions below give negative answers to both questions. The first has the Schur property and fails the Radon–Nikodým property, so it also shows why the latter hypothesis in the Lewis–Stegall theorem cannot be replaced by the Schur property.

There is a Dunford–Pettis projection \(P\) on \(L_1[0,1]\) with \(\lVert P\rVert\le4+3\sqrt2\). Its range has the Schur property but fails the Radon–Nikodým property. In particular, it is not isomorphic to any Banach lattice.

Changing the parameters in the same construction gives the non-Schur example. Its proof is given in Section 5.

There is a projection \(Q\) on \(L_1[0,1]\), with \(\lVert Q\rVert\le4+3\sqrt2\), whose range contains an isomorphic copy of \(\ell_2\) but no isomorphic copy of \(L_1[0,1]\). In particular, its range does not have the Schur property and is not isomorphic to any Banach lattice.

Both constructions are based on product measures on the countable sign group, a setting with antecedents in Rosenthal’s biased-coin construction ; see also . In the Schur example, we use singular convolution measures whose operators are Dunford–Pettis, a combination already present in work of Costé and Uhl. Schachermayer  discusses these antecedents and constructs singular measures whose convolution operators are compact on \(L_2\). This compactness is also the ingredient we use to establish the Dunford–Pettis property of the blocks of our projection.

The two examples introduce the general construction of Section 3. With suitable choices of the sequence \(\lambda=(\lambda_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}\), it produces a much larger family of complemented subspaces. Put \(\mathfrak c=2^{\aleph_0}\).

There is a family \((X_A)_{A\in\mathcal A}\), with \(|\mathcal A|=\mathfrak c\), of Banach spaces isometric to ranges of projections on \(L_1[0,1]\) of norm at most \(4+3\sqrt2\). If \(A,B\in\mathcal A\) are distinct, then \(X_A\) is not isomorphic to a subspace of \(X_B\).

As in Theorem A, each space \(X_A\) has the Schur property but fails the Radon–Nikodým property. In particular, none is isomorphic to a Banach lattice.

The separation of these spaces also gives information about closed operator ideals. Johnson, Pisier and Schechtman  constructed continuum many norm-closed two-sided ideals in \(\mathcal L(L_1[0,1])\), all contained in the strictly singular operators. Johnson and Schechtman  obtained \(2^{\mathfrak c}\) closed ideals for \(L_p[0,1]\) when \(1<p<\infty\) and \(p\ne2\); their later account  leaves open whether \(\mathcal L(L_1[0,1])\) has more than continuum many. The next theorem gives the maximal cardinality in this case.

There is a family \((\mathscr J_{\mathcal S})_{\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal A}\) of proper norm-closed two-sided ideals in \(\mathcal L(L_1[0,1])\) such that \[\mathscr J_{\mathcal S}\subseteq\mathscr J_{\mathcal T} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal T.\] In particular, \(\mathcal L(L_1[0,1])\) has exactly \(2^{\mathfrak c}\) norm-closed two-sided ideals.

These ideals are contained in the Dunford–Pettis ideal and are generated by projections with ranges isometric to the spaces in Theorem C. Every nonempty \(\mathcal S\) gives an ideal containing an infinite-rank projection.

The passage from an almost-disjoint family to many closed ideals follows the method of Johnson and Schechtman . Here the required separation comes from an entropy estimate for the product measures. We use it to control averaged differences along finite partitions after arbitrary bounded operators, and then pass this control to maps into the projection ranges.

Section 3 begins with probability distributions of infinitely many independent biased signs. These form a convolution semigroup; see Lemma 3.1. We take their exponential averages, called resolvent measures; Proposition 3.2 gives the identities satisfied by the associated convolution operators. We then define a function space by summing weighted errors between a function and its averaged versions. Lemma 3.3 establishes its basic properties, and Proposition 3.5 realises it as a complemented subspace of an \(L_1\)-space.

For the Schur example, two properties of these averages play distinct roles. By Lemma 4.1, all the distributions give full measure to the same Haar-null set, so their exponential averages remain singular. Proposition 4.2 shows that the associated convolution operators are nevertheless compact on \(L_2\). This compactness yields the Schur property through Liu’s band theorem , as shown in Proposition 4.3. Singularity obstructs the Radon–Nikodým property through Costé’s nonrepresentability result in Lemma 2.2, as explained in the proof of Theorem A. The lattice obstruction follows from the structural result of de Hevia et al. , which is also used for Theorem B.

In Section 5, we use the same bias in every coordinate. The general projection applies, and the coordinate functions span a copy of \(\ell_2\). Bonami’s estimate, the Enflo–Starbird criterion and Liu’s second band theorem  exclude copies of \(L_1\) from the range, proving Theorem B. Section 6 then proves Theorems C and D. Proposition 6.2 supplies the operator estimates, and Propositions 6.3 and 6.4 separate the members of the new family. Section 7 gives an interpolation interpretation of the general construction.

2.

Preliminaries

−

We write \(\mathbb N=\{1,2,\ldots\}\) and \(\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). All Banach spaces are over a fixed field \(\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}\), and an operator means a bounded linear map. For a Banach space \(Z\), \(\mathcal L(Z)\) denotes the Banach space of operators \(T\colon Z\to Z\), equipped with the operator norm. The symbols \(B_Z\) and \(S_Z\) denote the closed unit ball and unit sphere of \(Z\), respectively. The identity operator on \(Z\) is denoted by \(I_Z\), or simply \(I\) when the space is clear. The measures underlying \(L_p\)-spaces are completed; products and convolutions are formed from Borel measures.

We use standard Banach lattice terminology; see Schaefer  and Meyer-Nieberg . We recall a few notions used below. A real Banach lattice \(Z\) is order complete if every nonempty subset that is bounded above has a supremum. An order ideal in \(Z\) is a vector subspace \(I\subset Z\) such that \(x\in I\) and \(\lvert y\rvert\le\lvert x\rvert\) imply \(y\in I\). A band is an order ideal closed under suprema of increasing nets of its positive elements, whenever these suprema exist in \(Z\). An operator \(T\) between real Banach lattices is positive if \(Tx\ge0\) whenever \(x\ge0\), and \(S\le T\) means that \(T-S\) is positive. For a real \(L_1\)-space \(Z\), this order makes \(\mathcal L(Z)\) an order-complete Banach lattice; see .

An operator is Dunford–Pettis if it sends weakly null sequences to norm-null sequences. A Banach space has the Schur property if every weakly null sequence in it is norm null.

Let \((S,\eta)\) be a probability space and let \(Z\) be a Banach space. An operator \(T\colon L_1(S,\eta)\to Z\) is representable if there is an essentially bounded, strongly measurable function \(b\colon S\to Z\) with \[Tf=\int_S f(s)b(s)\,d\eta(s)\qquad(f\in L_1(S,\eta)),\] where the integral is a Bochner integral. Postcomposition with an operator preserves representability.

We will obtain the Dunford–Pettis property by checking compactness on bounded functions. We use the standard compact-restriction criterion in the following form; see .

Let \((S,\eta)\) be a standard nonatomic probability space. If \(T\colon L_1(S,\eta)\to Z\) has compact restriction to \(L_\infty(S,\eta)\), then \(T\) is Dunford–Pettis.

We work on the compact group \(G=\{-1,1\}^{\mathbb N}\), with coordinatewise multiplication and Haar probability measure \(m\). For a finite scalar Borel measure \(\tau\) on \(G\), the convolution operator \(T_\tau\colon L_1(G,m)\to L_1(G,m)\) is defined by \[T_\tau f(x)=(f*\tau)(x)=\int_G f(xy^{-1})\,d\tau(y), \qquad f\in L_1(G,m).\] When \(\tau\) is a probability measure, \(T_\tau f\) averages translates of \(f\) according to \(\tau\). Haar invariance and Fubini’s theorem make this definition independent of the Borel representative of \(f\), and \(\lVert T_\tau\rVert\le\lVert \tau\rVert\), where the latter norm is total variation. For finite \(F\subset\mathbb N\), the Walsh character \(\chi_F(x)=\prod_{j\in F}x_j\) satisfies \(T_\tau\chi_F=\widehat\tau(F)\chi_F\), where \(\widehat\tau(F)=\int_G\chi_F\,d\tau\). Finite linear combinations of Walsh characters are called Walsh polynomials. They are dense in \(L_p(G,m)\) for \(1\le p<\infty\), and the Walsh characters form an orthonormal basis of \(L_2(G,m)\).

Costé’s theorem says that a scalar convolution operator on \(L_1\) of a compact metrizable abelian group is representable if and only if its measure is absolutely continuous with respect to Haar measure; see . We use the following consequence.

If \(\tau\) is a nonzero finite scalar Borel measure on \(G\), singular with respect to \(m\), then \(T_\tau\colon L_1(G,m)\to L_1(G,m)\) is not representable.

A family \((\mu_u)_{u\ge0}\) of probability measures on \(G\) is a convolution semigroup if \(\mu_0=\delta_{\mathbf1}\) and \(\mu_u*\mu_v=\mu_{u+v}\) for \(u,v\ge0\). We assume that \(u\mapsto\mu_u(D)\) is measurable for every Borel set \(D\). The associated operator semigroup \((C_u)_{u\ge0}\), where \(C_u=T_{\mu_u}\), is assumed to be strongly continuous on \(L_1(G,m)\), meaning that \(C_uf\to f\) in \(L_1(G,m)\) as \(u\downarrow0\) for every \(f\in L_1(G,m)\). For \(t>0\), the normalised resolvent measure and its convolution operator are \[ \nu_t(D)=\int_0^\infty\mu_u(D)t^{-1}e^{-u/t}\,du, \qquad R_t=T_{\nu_t}. \](2.1) Thus, for \(f\in L_1(G,m)\), \[R_tf=\int_0^\infty t^{-1}e^{-u/t}C_uf\,du,\] where the latter integral is a Bochner integral. The exponential weight has integral one, so \(\nu_t\) is a probability measure and \(R_t\) is a positive contraction on every \(L_p(G,m)\). If \(-A\) denotes the generator of \((C_u)_{u\ge0}\) on \(L_1(G,m)\), then \[R_t=t^{-1}(t^{-1}I+A)^{-1}=(I+tA)^{-1}.\] The factor \(t^{-1}\) accounts for the normalisation of the usual resolvent at \(t^{-1}\). We refer to \(R_t\) simply as a resolvent below.

3.

The general construction

−

Fix a sequence \(\lambda=(\lambda_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}\) of nonnegative real numbers. We use this sequence to construct probability distributions of infinitely many independent biased signs. We shall specify \(\lambda\) in Sections 4 and 5 to obtain the Schur and non-Schur examples, respectively. For finite \(F\subset\mathbb N\), put \(\lambda_F=\sum_{j\in F}\lambda_j\). For \(u\ge0\), set \[ p_j(u)=\frac{1+e^{-u\lambda_j}}2\quad(j\in\mathbb N),\qquad \mu_u=\bigotimes_{j\in\mathbb N} \bigl(p_j(u)\delta_1+(1-p_j(u))\delta_{-1}\bigr). \](3.1) Each factor is a probability measure on \(\{-1,1\}\), so the countable product-measure theorem gives a unique Borel probability measure \(\mu_u\) on \(G\). Under \(\mu_u\), the coordinates are independent, and the \(j\)th sign equals \(1\) with probability \(p_j(u)\) and \(-1\) with probability \(1-p_j(u)\). In particular, its mean is \[ \int_G x_j\,d\mu_u(x)=2p_j(u)-1=e^{-u\lambda_j} \qquad(j\in\mathbb N,\ u\ge0). \](3.2)

A cylinder set in \(G\) is a set whose membership depends on only finitely many coordinates. For finite \(F\subset\mathbb N\) and \(\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_j)_{j\in F}\in\{-1,1\}^F\), the basic cylinder \[D(F,\varepsilon)=\{x\in G:x_j=\varepsilon_j\text{ for every }j\in F\}\] prescribes the signs on \(F\) and leaves all other coordinates unrestricted. Every cylinder set is a finite disjoint union of basic cylinders with a common coordinate set. For each \(u\ge0\) and cylinder set \(D\), the number \(\mu_u(D)\) is called the cylinder probability of \(D\) under \(\mu_u\). For a basic cylinder, independence gives \[ \mu_u\bigl(D(F,\varepsilon)\bigr) =\prod_{j\in F}\frac{1+\varepsilon_j e^{-u\lambda_j}}2. \](3.3) The cylinder sets form an algebra generating the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra of \(G\).

A family \((\mu_u)_{u\ge0}\) of Borel probability measures on \(G\) is a probability kernel if \(u\mapsto\mu_u(D)\) is Borel measurable on \([0,\infty)\) for every Borel set \(D\subset G\).

The measures in (3.1) and the operators \(C_u=T_{\mu_u}\) have the following properties.

  1. For every cylinder set \(D\), the map \(u\mapsto\mu_u(D)\) is continuous on \([0,\infty)\), and \((\mu_u)_{u\ge0}\) is a probability kernel.

  2. We have \(\mu_0=\delta_{\mathbf1}\) and \[\mu_u*\mu_v=\mu_{u+v}\qquad(u,v\ge0).\]

  3. Each \(C_u\) is a positive contraction on \(L_p(G,m)\) for \(1\le p\le\infty\).

  4. For finite \(F\subset\mathbb N\), \[C_u\chi_F=e^{-u\lambda_F}\chi_F.\]

  5. The semigroup \((C_u)_{u\ge0}\) is strongly continuous on \(L_p(G,m)\) for every \(1\le p<\infty\).

ProofFold proof

Proof. For (1), the right-hand side of (3.3) is a finite product of continuous functions of \(u\). Finite disjoint unions therefore give continuity of \(u\mapsto\mu_u(D)\) for every cylinder set \(D\). Let \(\mathcal D\) be the collection of Borel sets \(D\subset G\) for which \(u\mapsto\mu_u(D)\) is Borel measurable. This collection contains the cylinder sets and is closed under complements, since \(\mu_u(G\setminus D)=1-\mu_u(D)\). If \((D_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) is a pairwise disjoint sequence in \(\mathcal D\), then \[\mu_u\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}D_n\right) =\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mu_u(D_n)\] is measurable as a pointwise limit of measurable partial sums. Thus \(\mathcal D\) is a Dynkin system containing the cylinder algebra. The \(\pi\)–\(\lambda\) theorem gives \(\mathcal D=\mathcal B(G)\), proving the probability-kernel property.

For (2), at \(u=0\) every coordinate is \(1\) almost surely, so \(\mu_0=\delta_{\mathbf1}\). Take independent random elements \(X=(X_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}\) and \(Y=(Y_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}\) of \(G\), with probability distributions \(\mu_u\) and \(\mu_v\), respectively. Their coordinatewise product \(XY\) has probability distribution \(\mu_u*\mu_v\). Its coordinates are independent, and \[\mathbb E[X_jY_j]=\mathbb E[X_j]\mathbb E[Y_j] =e^{-u\lambda_j}e^{-v\lambda_j} =e^{-(u+v)\lambda_j}\qquad(j\in\mathbb N).\] The probability distribution of a sign is determined by its mean, so \(XY\) has probability distribution \(\mu_{u+v}\).

For (3), positivity of \(C_u\) follows from its definition as an average of translates. For \(1\le p<\infty\), Jensen’s inequality and Haar invariance give \[\lVert C_uf\rVert_p^p \le\int_G\int_G|f(xy^{-1})|^p\,d\mu_u(y)\,dm(x) =\lVert f\rVert_p^p.\] For \(p=\infty\), the same averaging formula gives \(\lVert C_uf\rVert_\infty\le\lVert f\rVert_\infty\).

For (4), independence and (3.2) give \[C_u\chi_F(x) =\chi_F(x)\int_G\prod_{j\in F}y_j\,d\mu_u(y) =\chi_F(x)\prod_{j\in F}e^{-u\lambda_j}.\]

For (5), part (4) gives \(C_uw\to w\) in \(L_p(G,m)\) as \(u\downarrow0\) for each Walsh polynomial \(w\) and \(1\le p<\infty\). For arbitrary \(f\in L_p(G,m)\), the contractivity in (3) gives \[\lVert C_uf-f\rVert_p \le 2\lVert f-w\rVert_p+\lVert C_uw-w\rVert_p.\] Choose \(w\) so that the first term is arbitrarily small, and then let \(u\downarrow0\). Density of Walsh polynomials proves convergence for every \(f\). Parts (2) and (3) extend continuity from zero to every \(u\ge0\). ◻

Let \(\nu_t\) and \(R_t\) be the resolvent measures and operators defined in (2.1), and write \(S_n=R_{2^{-n}}\) for \(n\in\mathbb N_0\). The following properties will be used in the construction of the projection.

For every finite \(F\subset\mathbb N\) and \(t>0\), \[ R_t\chi_F=(1+t\lambda_F)^{-1}\chi_F. \](3.4) The operators \(R_t\) commute, and \(R_t\xrightarrow{\mathrm{SOT}}I\) on \(L_1(G,m)\) as \(t\downarrow0\). For \(s,t>0\), \[ (I-R_s)R_t=\frac{s}{t}R_s(I-R_t),\qquad \lVert (I-R_s)R_t\rVert\le2\min\{1,s/t\}. \](3.5) Moreover, \[S_{n-1}(I-S_n)=S_n-S_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1).\]

ProofFold proof

Proof. Formula (3.4) follows from part (4) of Lemma 3.1 and (2.1). It also gives commutation on Walsh polynomials, and hence on \(L_1(G,m)\) by density and boundedness. For each finite \(F\subset\mathbb N\), the multiplier \((1+t\lambda_F)^{-1}\) tends to \(1\) as \(t\downarrow0\). Hence \(R_tw\to w\) in \(L_1(G,m)\) as \(t\downarrow0\) for every Walsh polynomial \(w\). For arbitrary \(f\in L_1(G,m)\) and any Walsh polynomial \(w\), contractivity gives \[\lVert R_tf-f\rVert_1 \le\lVert R_t(f-w)\rVert_1+\lVert R_tw-w\rVert_1+\lVert w-f\rVert_1 \le2\lVert f-w\rVert_1+\lVert R_tw-w\rVert_1.\] By density, we can first choose \(w\) so that \(\lVert f-w\rVert_1\) is arbitrarily small and then let \(t\downarrow0\). Thus \(R_tf\to f\) in \(L_1(G,m)\) as \(t\downarrow0\). The two identities hold on each Walsh character by the corresponding scalar identities, and therefore on every Walsh polynomial by linearity. By density and boundedness of the operators, they hold on all of \(L_1(G,m)\). The bound follows from contractivity and \(\lVert I-R_t\rVert\le2\). ◻

We first define the space \(\mathcal{X}_\lambda\) and then realise it isometrically as a complemented subspace of an \(L_1\)-space. Set \[ \mathcal{X}_\lambda=\{f\in L_1(G,m):\lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal{X}_\lambda}<\infty\},\qquad \lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal{X}_\lambda}=\lVert f\rVert_1+ \sum_{n=1}^\infty2^{n/2}\lVert (I-S_n)f\rVert_1. \](3.6) Let \(E_m\) be conditional expectation onto the first \(m\) coordinates of \(G\), with \(E_0f=(\int_G f\,dm)\mathbf1\). We begin by proving some elementary properties of \(\mathcal{X}_\lambda\).

The space \(\mathcal{X}_\lambda\) is a separable Banach space. Every finite-coordinate function belongs to \(\mathcal{X}_\lambda\), and these functions are dense in \(\mathcal{X}_\lambda\). The restrictions of \(E_m\) to \(\mathcal{X}_\lambda\) are contractive finite-rank projections and \(E_mf\to f\) in \(\mathcal{X}_\lambda\) for every \(f\in \mathcal{X}_\lambda\).

ProofFold proof

Proof. A Cauchy sequence in \(\mathcal{X}_\lambda\) has a limit \(f\) in \(L_1(G,m)\) and limits in the associated \(\ell_1\)-sum of difference coordinates. Boundedness of each \(I-S_n\) identifies these limits with \((I-S_n)f\), proving completeness. On any fixed finite-dimensional span of Walsh characters, \(\lVert I-S_n\rVert=O(2^{-n})\), so every finite-coordinate function belongs to \(\mathcal{X}_\lambda\). The operators \(E_m\) commute with \(S_n\) and are contractive on \(L_1(G,m)\), giving \(\lVert E_mf\rVert_{\mathcal{X}_\lambda}\le\lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal{X}_\lambda}\). For fixed \(f\in \mathcal{X}_\lambda\), every coordinate of its norm in (3.6) converges under \(E_m\), while the difference-coordinate tails are bounded by twice the corresponding summable tail for \(f\). Thus \(E_mf\to f\) in \(\mathcal{X}_\lambda\). This also proves density and separability. ◻

Put \(\mathcal E=\ell_1\bigl(\mathbb N_0;L_1(G,m)\bigr)\). This is an \(L_1\)-space: give \(\Omega=\mathbb N_0\times G\) the probability measure \(\rho(\{j\}\times D)=p_jm(D)\), where \(p_j=2^{-j-1}\), and use the surjective lattice isometry \[U\colon L_1(\Omega,\rho)\to\mathcal E,\qquad (Uh)_j=p_jh(j,\cdot) \quad(j\in\mathbb N_0).\] Partitioning \([0,1]\) into intervals of lengths \((p_j)_{j\in\mathbb N_0}\) and identifying each normalised interval with \(G\) by binary digits also gives a lattice isometry \(\mathcal E\cong L_1[0,1]\).

We will use this identification to apply two band theorems of Liu to the blocks of our projections. Write \(\mathcal E_{\mathbb R}\) for the real \(L_1\)-space just described and \(\Pi_i\) for its \(i\)th coordinate projection, \(i\in\mathbb N_0\). The next lemma shows that an operator belongs to a band whenever all of its blocks do.

Let \(\mathcal B\) be a band in \(\mathcal L(\mathcal E_{\mathbb R})\). If \(T\in\mathcal L(\mathcal E_{\mathbb R})\) and \(\Pi_iT\Pi_j\in\mathcal B\) for all \(i,j\in\mathbb N_0\), then \(T\in\mathcal B\).

ProofFold proof

Proof. The map \(S\mapsto\Pi_iS\Pi_j\) is a positive projection dominated by the identity on the operator lattice, hence a band projection. It therefore preserves moduli: \(|\Pi_iT\Pi_j|=\Pi_i|T|\Pi_j\). For \(N\in\mathbb N_0\), put \(H_N=\sum_{i=0}^N\Pi_i\). Then \[\sum_{i,j=0}^N|\Pi_iT\Pi_j|=H_N|T|H_N.\] Since each summand is positive and \(0\le H_N\le I\), these sums increase in the operator order and are bounded above by \(|T|\). Moreover, \(H_N|T|H_Nf\to|T|f\) in norm as \(N\to\infty\) for every \(f\ge0\), so their supremum is \(|T|\). Each finite sum belongs to \(\mathcal B\), so closure under order suprema gives \(|T|\), and hence \(T\), in \(\mathcal B\). ◻

The definition of the norm on \(\mathcal{X}_\lambda\) gives the isometric embedding \[ J\colon \mathcal{X}_\lambda\to\mathcal E,\qquad (Jf)_0=f,\qquad (Jf)_n=2^{n/2}(I-S_n)f\quad(n\ge1). \](3.7) To construct a projection onto its image, define \(K\colon\mathcal E\to L_1(G,m)\) by \[ Kx=S_0x_0+\sum_{n=1}^\infty2^{-n/2}S_{n-1}x_n \qquad(x=(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0}\in\mathcal E). \](3.8) Since the operators \(S_n\), \(n\in\mathbb N_0\), are contractions, the series converges absolutely in \(L_1(G,m)\) and \(\lVert K\rVert_{\mathcal E\to L_1(G,m)}\le1\).

The operator \(K\) takes values in \(\mathcal{X}_\lambda\). 6.1.

Averaged variation and entropy

Let \(\lambda=(\lambda_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}\) be a sequence of nonnegative real numbers. When several choices occur, we write \(C_u^\lambda\), \(R_t^\lambda\), \(J^\lambda\), \(K^\lambda\) and \(P^\lambda\) for the operators constructed in Section 3. The space \(\mathcal{X}_\lambda\) always carries the norm in (3.6). We first give a criterion that makes the average variation along a prescribed sequence of cylinder partitions vanish for every operator taking values in \(\mathcal{X}_\lambda\). The same partitions will later distinguish the different choices of \(\lambda\).

Fix positive integers \((k'_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\), and put \(M_0=0\) and \(M_n=\sum_{r=1}^n k'_r\) for \(n\in\mathbb N\). For \(\omega\in\{-1,1\}^{M_n}\), let \(A_{n,\omega}\) be the cylinder determined by \(\omega\) on the first \(M_n\) coordinates, and set \(e_{n,\omega}=2^{M_n}\mathbf 1_{A_{n,\omega}}\). At level zero, the only cylinder is \(G\) and its normalised indicator is \(\mathbf 1_G\). Every normalised indicator at level \(n-1\) is the average of its \(2^{k'_n}\) descendants at level \(n\).

For a Banach space \(Z\) and an operator \(T\colon L_1(G,m)\to Z\), define its averaged variation at level \(n\) by \[v_n(T)=2^{-M_n}\sum_{\omega\in\{-1,1\}^{M_n}} \lVert Te_{n,\omega} -Te_{n-1,\omega|_{M_{n-1}}}\rVert_Z \qquad(n\in\mathbb N).\] Fix also a strictly increasing sequence \((N_s)_{s\in\mathbb N}\) of positive integers. For every infinite set \(H\subseteq\mathbb N\), put \[p_H(T)=\limsup_{\substack{s\to\infty\\s\in H}} \frac1{N_s}\sum_{n=1}^{N_s}v_n(T).\] For each fixed target space, this is a seminorm satisfying \[ p_H(T)\le2\lVert T\rVert, \qquad p_H(WT)\le\lVert W\rVert p_H(T) \](6.1) whenever \(W\) is an operator defined on \(Z\). In particular, its kernel is a norm-closed linear space. These estimates follow directly from \(\lVert e_{n,\omega}\rVert_1=1\) and the triangle inequality.

For a nonnegative integrable function \(f\) with mass \(q=\int_G f\,dm\), write \[\operatorname{Ent}(f)=\int_G f\log(f/q)\,dm, \qquad \Phi(f)=\int_G f\log f\,dm.\] The first quantity is the entropy of \(f\) relative to \(m\), with value zero when \(q=0\), and \(0\log0\) is interpreted as zero. Thus \(\Phi(f)=\operatorname{Ent}(f)+q\log q\). For \(d\in\mathbb N_0\), set \(a_\lambda(d)=\inf_{j>d}\lambda_j\). The next lemma bounds the entropy after convolution by separating the first \(d\) coordinates from the remainder. Its proof uses entropy contraction under averaging coordinate projections, as in Caputo and Parisi . The second part converts entropy increments into variation estimates.

The result just proved applies to \(B_b\). The normalised indicators at each level average to \(\mathbf 1_G\), while \(C_\varepsilon^\lambda\) preserves the integral of nonnegative functions. Consequently, for every \(n\in\mathbb N\), \[v_n(C_\varepsilon^\lambda D_b) \le2\lVert D_b\mathbf 1_G\rVert_1 =2\int_{\{h>b\}}h\,dm.\] The right-hand side tends to zero as \(b\to\infty\). Subadditivity now proves \(p_H(C_\varepsilon^\lambda B)=0\) for every positive \(B\).

For a real operator \(B\), a positive decomposition can be obtained on the cylinder partitions already fixed. If \(A\) is an atom at level \(n\) and \(r\ge n\), set \[h_A^{(r)} =\sum_{\substack{\omega\in\{-1,1\}^{M_r}\\A_{r,\omega}\subseteq A}} \lvert B\mathbf 1_{A_{r,\omega}}\rvert.\] These functions increase with \(r\), and \(\lVert h_A^{(r)}\rVert_1\le\lVert B\rVert m(A)\). They therefore converge in \(L_1(G,m)\) to a nonnegative function \(h_A\) dominating \(\lvert B\mathbf 1_A\rvert\). The limits are additive under subdivision of \(A\), so \[B^+\mathbf 1_A=\tfrac12(h_A+B\mathbf 1_A), \qquad B^-\mathbf 1_A=\tfrac12(h_A-B\mathbf 1_A)\] define consistent positive maps on the union of the cylinder step functions. Both maps have norm at most \(\lVert B\rVert\) there. Since \(M_n\to\infty\), these step functions are dense in \(L_1(G,m)\). The maps extend to positive operators satisfying \(B=B^+-B^-\). Subadditivity gives the required conclusion for real \(B\). For complex \(B\), apply the real argument to the real and imaginary parts of \(B\) on real-valued functions. Every \(e_{n,\omega}\) is real-valued, so the triangle inequality gives the same conclusion.

To deduce part (1), split the defining resolvent integral at \(\varepsilon>0\) and use the semigroup identity: \[\lVert R_u^\lambda -e^{-\varepsilon/u}C_\varepsilon^\lambda R_u^\lambda\rVert \le1-e^{-\varepsilon/u}.\] The semigroup conclusion applies to the operator \(R_u^\lambda B\), and (6.1) gives \(p_H(R_u^\lambda B)\le2(1-e^{-\varepsilon/u})\lVert B\rVert\). Letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) proves part (1).

For part (2), put \(U=J^\lambda T\colon L_1(G,m)\to\mathcal E\). By Proposition 3.5, \(U=P^\lambda U\). Write \(U_i\) for the \(i\)th \(L_1(G,m)\) coordinate of \(U\). Set \(A_0^\lambda=I\) and \(A_i^\lambda=I-R_{2^{-i}}^\lambda\) for \(i\in\mathbb N\), and put \(\sigma_0=1\) and \(\sigma_j=2^{1-j}\) for \(j\in\mathbb N\). The block formula (3.9) gives \[U_i=\sum_{j=0}^\infty 2^{(i-j)/2}A_i^\lambda R_{\sigma_j}^\lambda U_j \qquad(i\in\mathbb N_0).\] For fixed \(i\), the block norms have a summable tail bounded by \(2^{(i-j)/2}\lVert A_i^\lambda\rVert\), so this series converges in operator norm. Part (1), the postcomposition estimate in (6.1) and norm closure imply \(p_H(U_i)=0\) for every \(i\in\mathbb N_0\).

To combine the coordinates, let \(F_m\colon\mathcal E\to\mathcal E\) retain coordinates \(0,\ldots,m\), for \(m\in\mathbb N_0\), and define \[h_n=\sum_{\omega\in\{-1,1\}^{M_n}} \lvert U\mathbf 1_{A_{n,\omega}}\rvert\in\mathcal E_+ \qquad(n\in\mathbb N_0),\] where the modulus is taken coordinatewise. Refinement makes \((h_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0}\) increasing, and the \(L_1\)-norm on \(\mathcal E\) gives \[\lVert h_n\rVert_\mathcal E =\sum_{\omega\in\{-1,1\}^{M_n}} \lVert U\mathbf 1_{A_{n,\omega}}\rVert_\mathcal E \le\lVert U\rVert.\] Monotone convergence in \(\mathcal E\) therefore gives \(h_n\to h\) in norm for some \(h\in\mathcal E_+\). Averaging the descendant and parent norms separately shows that \[v_n((I-F_m)U) \le\lVert (I-F_m)h_n\rVert_\mathcal E+\lVert (I-F_m)h_{n-1}\rVert_\mathcal E \le2\lVert (I-F_m)h\rVert_\mathcal E \qquad(n\in\mathbb N,\ m\in\mathbb N_0).\] The finitely many coordinates of \(F_mU\) have zero seminorm. It follows that \(p_H(U)\le2\lVert (I-F_m)h\rVert_\mathcal E\to0\) as \(m\to\infty\). Finally, \(J^\lambda\) is an isometry, so \(v_n(U)=v_n(T)\) for every \(n\in\mathbb N\), proving part (2). ◻

6.2.

The choice of parameters

−

We now choose one filtration for all the spaces. At each stage, the parameters will take one of two values. The smaller value preserves almost all the variation on that stage, whereas the larger value satisfies the entropy criterion. The proportion of levels belonging to the final stage tends to one.

Set \(D_0=N_0=0\). For \(s\in\mathbb N\), define \[ \begin{aligned} \ell_s&=(s!)^4,& h_s&=(s+1)^2\ell_s,& k_s&=\left\lceil64s^2e^{2s\ell_s}\right\rceil,\\ r_s&=s^2(D_{s-1}+1),& N_s&=N_{s-1}+r_s,& D_s&=D_{s-1}+r_sk_s. \end{aligned} \](6.3) Stage \(s\) consists of the \(r_s\) levels with \(N_{s-1}<n\le N_s\). At each of these levels, reveal \(k_s\) new coordinates. Thus the filtration used to define \(p_H\) is given by \[k_n'=k_s,\qquad M_n=D_{s-1}+(n-N_{s-1})k_s \qquad(N_{s-1}<n\le N_s),\] and \(M_{N_s}=D_s\).

The sequences in (6.3) satisfy \(\ell_s\le h_s<\ell_{s+1}\), and \((k_s)_{s\in\mathbb N}\) is increasing. Since \(N_{s-1}\le D_{s-1}\) and \(D_s/N_s\) is the average of \(k_1,\ldots,k_s\) with weights \(r_1,\ldots,r_s\), we have \[ \frac{D_{s-1}}{N_s}\le\frac1{s^2},\qquad \frac{r_s}{N_s}\ge\frac{s^2}{s^2+1},\qquad \frac{D_s}{N_s}\le k_s. \](6.4) Moreover, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), \[ k_se^{-\varepsilon h_s} \le65s^2\exp\bigl((2s-\varepsilon(s+1)^2)\ell_s\bigr) \longrightarrow0 \quad\text{as }s\to\infty. \](6.5)

For \(A\subseteq\mathbb N\), choose the parameters on stage \(s\) by \[ \lambda_j^A= \begin{cases} \ell_s,&s\in A,\\ h_s,&s\notin A \end{cases} \qquad(D_{s-1}<j\le D_s), \](6.6) and write \[X_A=\mathcal X_{\lambda^A}, \qquad R_A=R_1^{\lambda^A}.\] Each sequence \(\lambda^A=(\lambda_j^A)_{j\in\mathbb N}\) is nondecreasing and tends to infinity. For infinite \(A\), the seminorm \(p_A\) uses the endpoints \(N_s\) with \(s\in A\).

Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb N\) be infinite and let \(B\subseteq\mathbb N\) satisfy \(A\cap B\) finite. Then \[p_A(R_u^{\lambda^B}V)=0 \qquad\bigl(V\in\mathcal L(L_1(G,m)),\ u>0\bigr),\] and \(p_A(T)=0\) for every operator \(T\colon L_1(G,m)\to X_B\).

ProofFold proof

Proof. For all sufficiently large \(s\in A\), we have \(s\notin B\). Choose \(d_s=D_{s-1}\). By (6.6), all coordinates after \(d_s\) have parameters at least \(h_s\), since later stages have parameters at least \(\ell_{s+1}>h_s\). Consequently \(a_{\lambda^B}(d_s)\ge h_s\), and (6.4) gives \[\frac{d_s}{N_s}\le s^{-2},\qquad \frac{M_{N_s}}{N_s}e^{-\varepsilon a_{\lambda^B}(d_s)} \le k_se^{-\varepsilon h_s}.\] By (6.5), these are the limits required in (6.2) along \(A\). The two conclusions follow respectively from parts (1) and (2) of Proposition 6.2. ◻

For the same filtration, the resolvent associated with \(A\) has maximal variation along its own stages. The probability estimates in the proof will also provide a common Haar-null carrier.

For every infinite \(A\subseteq\mathbb N\), the operator \(R_A\colon L_1(G,m)\to L_1(G,m)\) satisfies \(\lVert R_A\rVert=1\) and \(p_A(R_A)=2\).

ProofFold proof

Proof. Positivity, contractivity and \(R_A\mathbf1=\mathbf1\) give \(\lVert R_A\rVert=1\). Fix \(s\in A\) and a level \(n\) in stage \(s\). The new coordinate block \(I_n=\{M_{n-1}+1,\ldots,M_n\}\) has size \(k_s\), and all its parameters are \(\ell_s\). Conditional expectation onto this block sends \[R_Ae_{n,\omega} -R_Ae_{n-1,\omega|_{\{1,\ldots,M_{n-1}\}}}\] to the density of the block marginal of the resolvent measure, translated by the signs of \(\omega\) on \(I_n\), minus \(\mathbf1\). Indeed, at every fixed time the density on the old coordinates has integral one, and this identity passes to the exponential average. Translations preserve the \(L_1\) norm, so it suffices to consider the pattern with every sign equal to \(1\).

Put \[q_s=e^{-s\ell_s},\qquad Z_{s,n}(x)=\frac1{k_s}\sum_{j\in I_n}x_j,\qquad E_{s,n}=\{Z_{s,n}>q_s/2\},\qquad \eta_s=\frac1{16s^2}.\] Under Haar measure, \(\mathbb E_m[Z_{s,n}]=0\) and \(\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_m(Z_{s,n})=1/k_s\). For \(0<t\le s\), independence gives \[\mathbb E_{\mu_t^{\lambda^A}}[Z_{s,n}] =e^{-t\ell_s}\ge q_s,\qquad \mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mu_t^{\lambda^A}}(Z_{s,n})\le\frac1{k_s}.\] Chebyshev’s inequality and the choice of \(k_s\) therefore imply \[ m(E_{s,n})\le\frac4{k_sq_s^2}\le\eta_s,\qquad \mu_t^{\lambda^A}(E_{s,n}^c)\le\frac4{k_sq_s^2}\le\eta_s \qquad(0<t\le s). \](6.7) The time-one resolvent measure \(\nu_1^{\lambda^A}\) consequently satisfies \[\nu_1^{\lambda^A}(E_{s,n})-m(E_{s,n}) \ge(1-e^{-s})(1-\eta_s)-\eta_s.\] Its marginal on \(I_n\) and Haar measure on this block are probability measures. The \(L_1\) distance between their densities is at least twice their difference on any event, and hence at least \[\delta_s=2\bigl((1-e^{-s})(1-\eta_s)-\eta_s\bigr) \longrightarrow2 \quad\text{as }s\to\infty.\] Contractivity of conditional expectation now gives \(v_n(R_A)\ge\delta_s\) at every level in stage \(s\). Thus, by (6.4), \[\frac1{N_s}\sum_{n=1}^{N_s}v_n(R_A) \ge\frac{r_s}{N_s}\delta_s\longrightarrow2 \quad\text{as }s\to\infty,\ s\in A.\] The reverse bound follows from \(p_A(R_A)\le2\lVert R_A\rVert=2\). ◻

The same probability estimates give a common carrier, which will provide the Radon–Nikodým obstruction for each space.

For every infinite \(A\subseteq\mathbb N\), there is a Borel set \(B_A\subseteq G\) such that \(m(B_A)=0\) and \(\mu_t^{\lambda^A}(B_A)=1\) for every \(t>0\).

ProofFold proof

Proof. For each \(s\in A\), use the first block of stage \(s\) and put \(E_s=E_{s,N_{s-1}+1}\), with the notation of Proposition 6.4. Define \[B_A=\bigcup_{r=1}^{\infty} \bigcap_{\substack{s\in A\\s\ge r}}E_s.\] By (6.7), \(\sum_{s\in A}m(E_s)\le\sum_{s=1}^{\infty}(16s^2)^{-1}<\infty\), so Borel–Cantelli gives \(m(B_A)=0\). 6.3.

The spaces and their ideals

−

An almost disjoint family is a family of infinite subsets of \(\mathbb N\) whose distinct members have finite intersection. We use the branches of the binary tree to obtain such a family of cardinality \(\mathfrak c\). Let \(2^{<\mathbb N}\) denote the set of finite binary sequences, and fix a bijection \(\iota\colon2^{<\mathbb N}\to\mathbb N\). For \(x=(x_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\), put \[A_x=\{\iota(x|_{\{1,\ldots,n\}}):n\in\mathbb N\},\qquad \mathcal A=\{A_x:x\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\}.\] Distinct branches share only finitely many initial segments. Consequently \(\mathcal A\) is almost disjoint and \(|\mathcal A|=\mathfrak c\).

Proof of Theorem CFold proof

Proof of Theorem C. For \(A\in\mathcal A\), Proposition 3.5 gives a projection \(P^{\lambda^A}\) on \(\mathcal E\) with range isometric to \(X_A\) and norm at most \(4+3\sqrt2\). Each \(X_A\) is infinite dimensional, since it contains all finite-coordinate functions by Lemma 3.3.

The compactness and band arguments from Propositions 4.2 and 4.3 apply whenever the parameters tend to infinity. Indeed, the Walsh eigenvalues \((1+t\sum_{j\in F}\lambda_j^A)^{-1}\) tend to zero off finite sets of finite subsets \(F\subseteq\mathbb N\), so \(R_t^{\lambda^A}\) is compact on \(L_2(G,m)\) for every \(t>0\). Each block of \(P^{\lambda^A}\) therefore has compact restriction to \(L_\infty(G,m)\) and is Dunford–Pettis by Lemma 2.1. Lemma 3.4 and Liu’s band theorem  make the real projection Dunford–Pettis; applying this to real and imaginary parts gives the complex case. Its range, and hence \(X_A\), has the Schur property.

By Lemma 6.5, the measure \(\nu_1^{\lambda^A}\) is singular with respect to \(m\). The map \(R_A\colon L_1(G,m)\to X_A\) is bounded, since it is the restriction of \(K^{\lambda^A}\) to the zeroth coordinate of \(\mathcal E\). If \(X_A\) had the Radon–Nikodým property, this map would be representable, and postcomposition with the continuous inclusion \(X_A\hookrightarrow L_1(G,m)\) would contradict Lemma 2.2, exactly as in the proof of Theorem A. Thus \(X_A\) fails the Radon–Nikodým property. The Banach lattice argument in that proof applies as well: over the reals, an isomorphism with a Banach lattice would make this complemented space isomorphic to an \(L_1\)-space by . Separability and infinite dimensionality then give either \(\ell_1\) or a copy of \(L_1[0,1]\), excluded respectively by failure of the Radon–Nikodým property and the Schur property. The same realification argument used there excludes complex Banach lattices.

Suppose that \(A,B\in\mathcal A\) are distinct and that \(S\colon X_A\to X_B\) is an isomorphic embedding. Choose \(c>0\) with \(\lVert Sf\rVert_{X_B}\ge c\lVert f\rVert_{X_A}\) for every \(f\in X_A\). Since \(\lVert f\rVert_{X_A}\ge\lVert f\rVert_1\), the definition of variation gives \[p_A(SR_A)\ge c\,p_A(R_A\colon L_1(G,m)\to L_1(G,m))=2c\] by Proposition 6.4. On the other hand, \(SR_A\colon L_1(G,m)\to X_B\) has zero seminorm by Proposition 6.3, a contradiction. Thus these spaces are mutually nonembedding. Finally, a fixed isometric identification of \(\mathcal E\) with \(L_1[0,1]\) gives the required complemented subspaces and their uniformly bounded projections. ◻

The same separation also distinguishes ideals generated by arbitrary subfamilies of the projections. We first describe them as ideals of operators factoring through the corresponding spaces.

Proof of Theorem DFold proof

Proof of Theorem D. For \(\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal A\), let \(\mathscr J_{\mathcal S}\) be the operator-norm closure in \(\mathcal L(L_1(G,m))\) of \[\left\{ \sum_{j=1}^{n}V_jU_j: \begin{array}{l} n\in\mathbb N_0,\ B_j\in\mathcal S,\\ U_j\colon L_1(G,m)\to X_{B_j},\ V_j\colon X_{B_j}\to L_1(G,m) \quad(1\le j\le n) \end{array} \right\}.\] The empty sum is zero. These finite sums form a two-sided ideal, and continuity of multiplication by a fixed operator shows that their norm closure is also a two-sided ideal.

Fix an isometric isomorphism \(W\colon\mathcal E\to L_1(G,m)\) and, for \(B\in\mathcal A\), put \[j_B=WJ^{\lambda^B},\qquad k_B=K^{\lambda^B}W^{-1},\qquad Q_B=WP^{\lambda^B}W^{-1}=j_Bk_B.\] Then \(k_Bj_B=I_{X_B}\) and \(\lVert Q_B\rVert\le4+3\sqrt2\). Every product \(UQ_BV\), with \(U,V\in\mathcal L(L_1(G,m))\), factors through \(X_B\). Conversely, for \(u\colon L_1(G,m)\to X_B\) and \(v\colon X_B\to L_1(G,m)\), \[vu=(vk_B)Q_B(j_Bu).\] Consequently \(\mathscr J_{\mathcal S}\) is precisely the norm-closed two-sided ideal generated by \(\{Q_B:B\in\mathcal S\}\).

If \(A\in\mathcal S\), the bounded factorization \(R_A\colon L_1(G,m)\to X_A\hookrightarrow L_1(G,m)\) gives \(R_A\in\mathscr J_{\mathcal S}\). If \(A\notin\mathcal S\), every \(B\in\mathcal S\) has finite intersection with \(A\). Proposition 6.3 and bounded postcomposition give \(p_A(VU)=0\) whenever \(U\colon L_1(G,m)\to X_B\) and \(V\colon X_B\to L_1(G,m)\). The same continuous seminorm \(p_A\) therefore vanishes on all the finite sums and on their norm closure. For \(F\in\mathscr J_{\mathcal S}\), Proposition 6.4 yields \[2=p_A(R_A)\le p_A(R_A-F)+p_A(F)\le2\lVert R_A-F\rVert.\] Since \(0\in\mathscr J_{\mathcal S}\) and \(\lVert R_A\rVert=1\), this proves \[\operatorname{dist}(R_A,\mathscr J_{\mathcal S})=1 \qquad(A\in\mathcal A\setminus\mathcal S).\] Inclusion of subfamilies implies inclusion of ideals. Conversely, if \(\mathcal S\not\subseteq\mathcal T\), choose \(A\in\mathcal S\setminus\mathcal T\). Then \(R_A\) belongs to \(\mathscr J_{\mathcal S}\) and has distance one from \(\mathscr J_{\mathcal T}\). Thus \(\mathcal S\mapsto\mathscr J_{\mathcal S}\) is an order embedding.

Every operator factoring through a Schur space is Dunford–Pettis, because a weakly null sequence is sent to a weakly null and hence norm-null sequence in that space. Dunford–Pettis operators form a norm-closed two-sided ideal, so every \(\mathscr J_{\mathcal S}\) is contained in this ideal. It is proper: the coordinate functions \((x\mapsto x_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}\) form a weakly null sequence of norm one in \(L_1(G,m)\), and hence its identity is not Dunford–Pettis. For nonempty \(\mathcal S\), any \(Q_B\) with \(B\in\mathcal S\) is an infinite-rank projection in \(\mathscr J_{\mathcal S}\).

There are \(2^{\mathfrak c}\) subfamilies of \(\mathcal A\), giving the stated lower bound, also after discarding the zero ideal. For the upper bound, \(L_1(G,m)\) is separable and has cardinality \(\mathfrak c\). An operator is determined by its values on a countable dense set, so \(|\mathcal L(L_1(G,m))|=\mathfrak c\) and there are at most \(2^{\mathfrak c}\) subsets of this operator space. The same conclusions hold on \(L_1[0,1]\) under an isometric identification with \(L_1(G,m)\). ◻

7.

An interpolation interpretation

−

We give an alternative interpretation of the general construction through real interpolation. The argument applies to any sequence \(\lambda=(\lambda_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}\) of nonnegative real numbers, as in Section 3. Let \(-A_\lambda\) be the generator of the associated semigroup \((C_u)_{u\ge0}\) on \(L_1(G,m)\), so that \(R_t=(I+tA_\lambda)^{-1}\), and give the domain of \(A_\lambda\), denoted by \(D(A_\lambda)\), its graph norm \(\lVert g\rVert_{D(A_\lambda)}=\lVert g\rVert_1+\lVert A_\lambda g\rVert_1\).

As spaces of functions, with equivalent norms, \[\mathcal{X}_\lambda=\bigl(L_1(G,m),D(A_\lambda)\bigr)_{1/2,1}.\]

ProofFold proof

Proof. Write \[\mathcal K(t,f)=\inf_{g\in D(A_\lambda)} \bigl(\lVert f-g\rVert_1+t\lVert g\rVert_{D(A_\lambda)}\bigr).\] For \(0<t\le1\), the resolvent identities give \[ \tfrac12\lVert (I-R_t)f\rVert_1 \le\mathcal K(t,f) \le2\lVert (I-R_t)f\rVert_1+t\lVert f\rVert_1. \](7.1) For the upper bound, take \(g=R_tf\) and use \(tA_\lambda R_t=I-R_t\) and contractivity. For the lower bound, apply \(I-R_t\) to \(f=(f-g)+g\) and use \(\lVert (I-R_t)g\rVert_1\le t\lVert A_\lambda g\rVert_1\). For \(t\ge1\), the graph norm dominates the \(L_1(G,m)\) norm, so \(\mathcal K(t,f)=\lVert f\rVert_1\). Since \(\mathcal K(t,f)\) is nondecreasing and \(\mathcal K(t,f)/t\) is nonincreasing, the interpolation integral is comparable with its dyadic samples: \[\int_0^\infty t^{-1/2}\mathcal K(t,f)\,\frac{dt}{t} \asymp\lVert f\rVert_1+ \sum_{n=1}^\infty2^{n/2}\mathcal K(2^{-n},f).\] Here \(\asymp\) means that each side is bounded by a positive constant multiple of the other, with constants independent of \(f\). Equation (7.1) and summability of \(2^{-n/2}\) identify this expression, up to fixed constants, with \(\lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal{X}_\lambda}\). ◻

In particular, this identifies \(\mathcal{CS}\) and \(\mathcal{RB}\) with the interpolation spaces corresponding to \(\lambda_j=\sqrt{\log(j+1)}\) and \(\lambda_j=1\) for \(j\in\mathbb N\), respectively.

For either choice of \(\lambda\), the retraction also applies on \(L_p(G,m)\), \(1\le p<\infty\). Let \(\mathcal{X}_{p,\lambda}\) consist of the functions \(f\in L_p(G,m)\) for which \[\lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal{X}_{p,\lambda}} =\left(\lVert f\rVert_p^p+ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}2^{np/2}\lVert (I-S_n)f\rVert_p^p\right)^{1/p} <\infty.\] Thus \(\mathcal{X}_{1,\lambda}=\mathcal{X}_\lambda\). The maps in (3.7)–(3.8) complement \(\mathcal{X}_{p,\lambda}\) in \(\mathcal E_p=\ell_p\bigl(\mathbb N_0;L_p(G,m)\bigr)\cong L_p[0,1]\): the geometric block estimates give uniformly bounded row and column sums. The preceding \(\mathcal K\)-functional argument identifies \(\mathcal{X}_{p,\lambda}=\bigl(L_p(G,m),D(A_{p,\lambda})\bigr)_{1/2,p}\) with equivalent norms, where \(-A_{p,\lambda}\) is the generator on \(L_p(G,m)\) and its domain is equipped with the graph norm.

For \(1<p<\infty\), it can be checked that the choice of \(\lambda\) from Section 4 gives \(\mathcal{X}_{p,\lambda}\cong\ell_p\). For \(\lambda_j=1\) for every \(j\in\mathbb N\), the space \(\mathcal{X}_{p,\lambda}\) contains a copy of \(\ell_2\) and is not isomorphic to \(\ell_p\) when \(p\ne2\). For both choices, all the ranges with \(1<p<\infty\) are reflexive and have the Radon–Nikodým property.

results.statementHtml: There is a Dunford–Pettis projection \(P\) on \(L_1[0,1]\) with \(\lVert P\rVert\le4+3\sqrt2\). Its range has the Schur property but fails the Radon–Nikodým property. In particular, it is not isomorphic to any Banach lattice.

There is a projection \(Q\) on \(L_1[0,1]\), with \(\lVert Q\rVert\le4+3\sqrt2\), whose range contains an isomorphic copy of \(\ell_2\) but no isomorphic copy of \(L_1[0,1]\). In particular, its range does not have the Schur property and is not isomorphic to any Banach lattice.

There is a family \((X_A)_{A\in\mathcal A}\), with \(|\mathcal A|=\mathfrak c\), of Banach spaces isometric to ranges of projections on \(L_1[0,1]\) of norm at most \(4+3\sqrt2\). If \(A,B\in\mathcal A\) are distinct, then \(X_A\) is not isomorphic to a subspace of \(X_B\).

There is a family \((\mathscr J_{\mathcal S})_{\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal A}\) of proper norm-closed two-sided ideals in \(\mathcal L(L_1[0,1])\) such that \[\mathscr J_{\mathcal S}\subseteq\mathscr J_{\mathcal T} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal T.\] In particular, \(\mathcal L(L_1[0,1])\) has exactly \(2^{\mathfrak c}\) norm-closed two-sided ideals.
Let \((S,\eta)\) be a standard nonatomic probability space. If \(T\colon L_1(S,\eta)\to Z\) has compact restriction to \(L_\infty(S,\eta)\), then \(T\) is Dunford–Pettis.
If \(\tau\) is a nonzero finite scalar Borel measure on \(G\), singular with respect to \(m\), then \(T_\tau\colon L_1(G,m)\to L_1(G,m)\) is not representable.

The measures in (3.1) and the operators \(C_u=T_{\mu_u}\) have the following properties.

  1. For every cylinder set \(D\), the map \(u\mapsto\mu_u(D)\) is continuous on \([0,\infty)\), and \((\mu_u)_{u\ge0}\) is a probability kernel.

  2. We have \(\mu_0=\delta_{\mathbf1}\) and \[\mu_u*\mu_v=\mu_{u+v}\qquad(u,v\ge0).\]

  3. Each \(C_u\) is a positive contraction on \(L_p(G,m)\) for \(1\le p\le\infty\).

  4. For finite \(F\subset\mathbb N\), \[C_u\chi_F=e^{-u\lambda_F}\chi_F.\]

  5. The semigroup \((C_u)_{u\ge0}\) is strongly continuous on \(L_p(G,m)\) for every \(1\le p<\infty\).

For every finite \(F\subset\mathbb N\) and \(t>0\), \[ R_t\chi_F=(1+t\lambda_F)^{-1}\chi_F. \](3.4) The operators \(R_t\) commute, and \(R_t\xrightarrow{\mathrm{SOT}}I\) on \(L_1(G,m)\) as \(t\downarrow0\). For \(s,t>0\), \[ (I-R_s)R_t=\frac{s}{t}R_s(I-R_t),\qquad \lVert (I-R_s)R_t\rVert\le2\min\{1,s/t\}. \](3.5) Moreover, \[S_{n-1}(I-S_n)=S_n-S_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1).\]

The space \(\mathcal{X}_\lambda\) is a separable Banach space. Every finite-coordinate function belongs to \(\mathcal{X}_\lambda\), and these functions are dense in \(\mathcal{X}_\lambda\). The restrictions of \(E_m\) to \(\mathcal{X}_\lambda\) are contractive finite-rank projections and \(E_mf\to f\) in \(\mathcal{X}_\lambda\) for every \(f\in \mathcal{X}_\lambda\).

Let \(\mathcal B\) be a band in \(\mathcal L(\mathcal E_{\mathbb R})\). If \(T\in\mathcal L(\mathcal E_{\mathbb R})\) and \(\Pi_iT\Pi_j\in\mathcal B\) for all \(i,j\in\mathbb N_0\), then \(T\in\mathcal B\).

The operator \(K\) takes values in \(\mathcal{X}_\lambda\). As a map \(K\colon\mathcal E\to\mathcal{X}_\lambda\), where the latter is equipped with the norm \(\lVert \cdot\rVert_{\mathcal{X}_\lambda}\) defined in (3.6), it satisfies \(\lVert K\rVert_{\mathcal E\to\mathcal{X}_\lambda}\le4+3\sqrt2\) and \(KJ=I_{\mathcal{X}_\lambda}\). Consequently \(P=JK\) is a projection on \(\mathcal E\) with \(\lVert P\rVert\le4+3\sqrt2\) and range \(J\mathcal{X}_\lambda\). Its zeroth diagonal block is \(P_{00}=R_1\).
There is a Borel set \(N\subset G\) such that \(m(N)=0\) and \(\mu_u(N)=1\) for every \(u>0\).
For every \(t>0\), the operator \(R_t\) is compact on \(L_2(G,m)\). Its restriction \(R_t\colon L_\infty(G,m)\to L_1(G,m)\) is also compact.
The projection \(P\) is Dunford–Pettis, and \(\mathcal{CS}\) has the Schur property.

Let \(T\colon L_1(G,m)\to L_1(G,m)\) be an operator over the real field. If \(\lVert Tf\rVert_2\le c\lVert f\rVert_p\) for every \(f\in L_p(G,m)\), where \(1<p<2\) and \(c>0\), then \(T\) is non-Enflo.

1. For every bounded nonnegative \(f\), \(d\in\mathbb N_0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), \[\operatorname{Ent}(C_\varepsilon^\lambda f) \le d(\log2)\lVert f\rVert_1 +e^{-\varepsilon a_\lambda(d)}\operatorname{Ent}(f).\]

  2. If \(f_1,\ldots,f_r\) are bounded nonnegative functions with masses at most one and \(g=r^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^r f_i\), then \[\frac1r\sum_{i=1}^r\Phi(f_i)-\Phi(g) \ge\frac1{4r}\sum_{i=1}^r\lVert f_i-g\rVert_1^2.\]

Let \(H\subseteq\mathbb N\) be infinite. Suppose that there are integers \((d_s)_{s\in H}\) in \(\mathbb N_0\) such that, as \(s\to\infty\) through \(H\), \[ \frac{d_s}{N_s}\longrightarrow0, \qquad \frac{M_{N_s}}{N_s}e^{-\varepsilon a_\lambda(d_s)} \longrightarrow0 \quad\text{for every }\varepsilon>0. \](6.2) Then the following hold.

  1. For every operator \(B\colon L_1(G,m)\to L_1(G,m)\) and every \(u>0\), \(p_H(R_u^\lambda B)=0\).

  2. For every operator \(T\colon L_1(G,m)\to\mathcal{X}_\lambda\), \(p_H(T)=0\).

Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb N\) be infinite and let \(B\subseteq\mathbb N\) satisfy \(A\cap B\) finite. Then \[p_A(R_u^{\lambda^B}V)=0 \qquad\bigl(V\in\mathcal L(L_1(G,m)),\ u>0\bigr),\] and \(p_A(T)=0\) for every operator \(T\colon L_1(G,m)\to X_B\).
For every infinite \(A\subseteq\mathbb N\), the operator \(R_A\colon L_1(G,m)\to L_1(G,m)\) satisfies \(\lVert R_A\rVert=1\) and \(p_A(R_A)=2\).
For every infinite \(A\subseteq\mathbb N\), there is a Borel set \(B_A\subseteq G\) such that \(m(B_A)=0\) and \(\mu_t^{\lambda^A}(B_A)=1\) for every \(t>0\).
As spaces of functions, with equivalent norms, \[\mathcal{X}_\lambda=\bigl(L_1(G,m),D(A_\lambda)\bigr)_{1/2,1}.\]

readingGlossary.title: Schur property
readingGlossary.html: A Banach space has the Schur property if every weakly convergent sequence converges in norm. Equivalently, every weakly null sequence is norm-null.

readingGlossary.title: The spaces 𝒳λ
readingGlossary.html: \(\mathcal X_\lambda\) is the space of functions whose weighted errors under the resolvent averages are summable. The sequence \(\lambda\) determines those averages. Section 3 gives its norm and constructs the projection onto an isometric copy of this space.

readingGlossary.title: The ideal 𝒥𝒮
readingGlossary.html: \(\mathscr J_{\mathcal S}\) is the norm-closed two-sided ideal generated by the projections corresponding to the subfamily \(\mathcal S\). Theorem D shows that inclusion of these ideals records inclusion of the subfamilies.
